title: OA 2 — Risk, Classification, and Experimentation
description: Mock data-science internship assessment: logistic regression, trees and confusion matrices, hypothesis testing and A/B experiments, responsible AI, risk-alert SQL (Accounts / Transactions / AccountProfiles / RiskAlerts), transaction feature engineering in pandas, and string/hash-map and greedy-interval DSA.
disclaimer: Independent practice material informed by publicly reported role requirements and general internship-assessment patterns. Not official Nasdaq questions.

revealPolicy.rule: Never send private fields to the candidate's browser; reveal solutions only after the whole attempt has been submitted or timed out.

questions.statement: A logistic regression for card fraud has a coefficient of +0.69 on the feature 'number of foreign transactions in the last 24 h' (all other features held fixed). How is this coefficient best interpreted?

options.text: Each additional foreign transaction multiplies the odds of fraud by about 2 (e^0.69 ≈ 2)
Each additional foreign transaction multiplies the probability of fraud by about 2
The feature explains 69% of the variance in fraud
Each additional foreign transaction raises the probability of fraud by 0.69

solution.explanation: Logistic regression is linear in the log-odds, so a coefficient β multiplies the odds by e^β per unit increase. The effect on probability is not constant (it depends on the baseline), and the coefficient is not a variance-explained measure.

questions.statement: A node has 50 fraud and 50 legitimate samples (Gini = 0.5). Split A sends 40 fraud + 10 legit left and 10 fraud + 40 legit right. Split B sends 30 fraud + 20 legit left and 20 fraud + 30 legit right. Which split does a Gini-based tree prefer?

options.text: Split B, with weighted child Gini 0.32
Neither: both give the same impurity as the parent
Split A, with weighted child Gini 0.32 versus 0.48 for split B
Split B, because its children are larger and therefore more stable

solution.explanation: Gini of a child = 1 − Σp². Split A children: 1 − (0.8² + 0.2²) = 0.32 each → weighted 0.32. Split B: 1 − (0.6² + 0.4²) = 0.48. The lower weighted impurity (larger impurity decrease) wins.

questions.statement: A fraud model outputs probabilities. The risk team says missing a real fraud case is far more costly than reviewing a legitimate one. What should happen to the classification threshold, and what is the typical consequence?

options.text: Lower the threshold: precision rises and recall usually falls
Keep 0.5, since the threshold has no effect on recall
Raise the threshold: recall rises and precision usually falls
Lower the threshold: recall rises and precision usually falls

solution.explanation: Flagging more cases (lower cut-off) catches more true frauds (higher recall) at the cost of more false positives (lower precision). Raising the threshold does the opposite.

questions.statement: A classifier has ROC AUC = 0.82 on a held-out set. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The model has a precision of 0.82 at the 0.5 threshold
If you pick one random positive and one random negative case, the model scores the positive higher about 82% of the time
82% of all predictions are correct at every threshold
The model is guaranteed to be calibrated

solution.explanation: AUC is the probability that a random positive is ranked above a random negative. It is threshold-independent, says nothing about precision at a specific cut-off, and does not imply calibrated probabilities.

questions.statement: A team tries 200 hyper-parameter settings, picks the one with the best score on the test set, and reports that score as the expected production performance. What is wrong?

options.text: Hyper-parameters should never be tuned
Nothing; more tuning always yields an unbiased estimate
The model must be retrained on the test set to be fair
The test set was used for model selection, so the reported score is optimistically biased; tune on a validation set or with CV and keep the test set untouched

solution.explanation: Selecting the best of many candidates on the same data exploits chance fluctuations. A final untouched test set (or nested CV) is needed for an unbiased estimate.

questions.statement: A logistic regression without regularization is fitted to training data in which one feature perfectly separates the two classes. What typically happens?

options.text: The coefficient converges to exactly 1
The loss becomes negative
The model automatically drops that feature
The maximum-likelihood coefficient grows without bound (the optimiser does not converge to a finite solution); a regularization penalty keeps it finite

solution.explanation: With perfect separation the likelihood keeps improving as the weight grows, so no finite maximiser exists. L2 (or L1) regularization adds a penalty that yields finite coefficients.

questions.statement: In a test of whether a new fraud rule changes the alert rate, you obtain p = 0.03. Which interpretation is correct?

options.text: There is a 3% probability that the null hypothesis is true
The effect size is 3%
There is a 97% probability that the rule works
If the rule truly had no effect, results at least as extreme as those observed would occur about 3% of the time

solution.explanation: A p-value is computed assuming H0 is true: P(data this extreme | H0). It is not the probability that H0 is true or that the alternative holds, and it says nothing about effect magnitude.

questions.statement: With the sample size fixed, an analyst reduces the significance level from α = 0.05 to α = 0.01. What is the usual effect?

options.text: Type I error increases and power increases
Neither changes unless the sample size changes
Both Type I and Type II error rates decrease
Type I error rate decreases and Type II error rate increases (power decreases)

solution.explanation: A stricter α demands stronger evidence to reject H0: fewer false positives but more missed true effects (lower power) for a given n and effect size.

questions.statement: To detect a true mean shift of 2 units with a one-sample two-sided z-test (σ = 10, α = 0.05, desired power 80%, z-values 1.96 and 0.84), what sample size is needed?

solution.explanation: n = ((z_{α/2} + z_β)·σ/δ)² = ((1.96 + 0.84)·10/2)² = 14² = 196. 784 would result from using δ = 1; 49 from forgetting to square the (σ/δ) ratio correctly.

questions.statement: In an A/B test, control converted 200 of 2,000 users (10%) and treatment 240 of 2,000 (12%). Using a pooled two-proportion z-test, what is the z statistic (approximately) and the conclusion at α = 0.05 (two-sided)?

options.text: z ≈ 0.02, so the difference is not significant
z ≈ 2.02, so the difference is statistically significant
z ≈ 4.0, so the difference is significant
z ≈ 2.02, so the difference is not significant because the critical value is 2.58

questions.statement: For two events: P(Flagged) = 0.30, P(High-value) = 0.50 and P(Flagged and High-value) = 0.15. Which statement is correct?

options.text: They are independent because P(A) + P(B) < 1
They are dependent, because P(A∩B) is not zero
They are independent, because P(A∩B) = P(A)·P(B) = 0.15
They are mutually exclusive, because 0.15 is small

solution.explanation: Independence means P(A∩B) = P(A)P(B); here 0.3 × 0.5 = 0.15. Mutually exclusive events would have P(A∩B) = 0 (and are then dependent, unless one has probability 0).

questions.statement: A loan model approves 60% of applicants from group X and 40% from group Y, but among truly creditworthy applicants both groups are approved at the same rate (equal true positive rate). Which statement is accurate?

options.text: Neither fairness criterion holds
Equal opportunity (equal TPR) holds, but demographic parity (equal approval rates) does not
Demographic parity holds because the TPRs match
Both demographic parity and equal opportunity hold

solution.explanation: Demographic parity compares overall positive-decision rates (60% vs 40% → violated). Equal opportunity compares TPR among truly positive individuals (equal → satisfied). Different fairness criteria can disagree, so the choice must be justified for the use case.

questions.statement: A team removes the protected attribute 'gender' from a credit model's inputs and claims the model is now unbiased. Why is that claim weak?

options.text: Removing a feature can never change a model's predictions
Other features (e.g., occupation or purchase categories) can act as proxies for gender, so disparities can persist; fairness must be measured on outcomes
Protected attributes are always the most predictive features, so removal is impossible
Fairness only matters for neural networks

solution.explanation: 'Fairness through unawareness' fails when other variables are correlated with the protected attribute. Auditing outcomes (e.g., approval and error rates by group) is required.

questions.statement: A customer disputes why their individual transaction was blocked. Which kind of explanation best serves this request?

options.text: The list of all hyper-parameters
A local, per-prediction explanation (e.g., SHAP values or a counterfactual: "approved if amount were below X")
The model's overall accuracy on the test set
A global feature-importance bar chart averaged over all customers

solution.explanation: The question concerns one decision, so a local explanation that attributes that single prediction (or offers a counterfactual) is appropriate. Global importance describes the model on average and does not justify one decision.

questions.statement: While training a neural network, training loss keeps decreasing but validation loss starts increasing after epoch 12. What is the standard remedy?

options.text: Increase the learning rate to reduce the training loss faster
Train for many more epochs until the validation loss comes down by itself
Evaluate only on the training data from now on
Stop at (or restore weights from) about epoch 12 – early stopping – and/or add regularization such as dropout

solution.explanation: Diverging validation loss indicates overfitting. Early stopping and regularization limit memorisation; training longer or ignoring validation performance makes it worse.

questions.statement: A composite index exists on Transactions(account_id, txn_time). Which query can use the index efficiently for an index range scan?

options.text: WHERE txn_time >= '2025-01-01' (no condition on account_id)
WHERE account_id = 42 AND txn_time >= '2025-01-01'
WHERE amount > 1000
WHERE txn_time = '2025-01-01' OR amount > 5

solution.explanation: A B-tree composite index is ordered by its leading column first. Seeking on account_id and then ranging on txn_time uses it fully; predicates that skip the leading column or involve other columns cannot use it for a seek (leftmost-prefix rule).

questions.statement: A funds transfer runs two UPDATEs (debit account A, credit account B). The system crashes after the first UPDATE but before the second. Which ACID property ensures the debit is rolled back?

options.text: Consistency of the index
Isolation
Atomicity
Durability

solution.explanation: Atomicity means a transaction is all-or-nothing: if it cannot complete, its partial changes are undone. Isolation concerns concurrent transactions; durability guarantees that committed data survives crashes.
`a / 2` is integer division (both operands are int) giving 3 before it is widened to double 3.0. Writing `a / 2.0` would give 3.5.

questions.statement: A `RiskReport` class needs the ability to format numbers using the existing `Formatter` class. Which design is generally preferable?

options.text: Copy the Formatter code into every report class
Give RiskReport a Formatter field (composition), because a report is not a kind of formatter
Make RiskReport extend Formatter, since this reuses the code
Make all Formatter methods static and extend them in each report

solution.explanation: Inheritance should model an 'is-a' relationship; reuse alone is better achieved by composition ('has-a'), which keeps coupling lower and avoids exposing unrelated inherited methods.

questions.statement: A KYC form accepts ages 18–65 inclusive. Using equivalence partitioning, what is the minimum number of test cases to cover every equivalence class (one representative each)?

options.text: 3 (below 18, 18–65, above 65)

solution.explanation: There are three classes: invalid-low, valid, invalid-high; each class needs one representative. Boundary-value analysis would add edge cases (17, 18, 65, 66) on top of this.

questions.statement: Cells A2:A5 contain B1, B2, B3, B4 and C2:C5 contain 10, 20, 30, 40. What does =INDEX(C2:C5, MATCH("B3", A2:A5, 0)) return?

options.text: #N/A
B3

solution.explanation: MATCH with match type 0 finds the exact position of "B3" in A2:A5 (3rd item); INDEX then returns the 3rd value in C2:C5, i.e., 30. The position (3) is only the intermediate result.

questions.statement: A fraud rule flags any transaction with amount > 10,000. The Transactions table stores 'amount' in the transaction's local currency (USD, EUR, JPY) without conversion. What is the most likely data-quality problem?

options.text: Nothing; amounts in different currencies are directly comparable
The threshold should be compared with the account number instead
Mixed currencies make the threshold inconsistent: many ordinary JPY transactions are flagged while large USD/EUR ones may not be; amounts should be normalised to a common currency first
Currencies only matter for date columns

solution.explanation: 10,000 JPY is under $100 whereas 10,000 USD is a large payment. Comparing raw amounts across currencies produces false positives and false negatives, so convert using dated FX rates (or store a normalised amount) before applying thresholds.

questions.title: January Spending of Active Accounts
questions.statement:
Compliance wants to review heavy January 2025 activity.

Join `Accounts` and `Transactions` and return, for every account whose `status = 'ACTIVE'`:

`account_id, customer_name, txn_count, total_amount, largest_txn`

Only count **purchases** (`amount > 0`; refunds are negative) made in January 2025, i.e. `txn_time` from `'2025-01-01 00:00:00'` up to but **excluding** `'2025-02-01 00:00:00'`. Return only accounts with **at least 3** such purchases. `total_amount` is `SUM(amount)` rounded to 2 decimals and `largest_txn` the maximum amount. Sort by `total_amount` descending, then `account_id` ascending.

tables.name: Transactions
tables.description: Card/bank transactions; negative amounts are refunds.

questions.schemaSql:
CREATE TABLE Accounts (
  account_id    INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  customer_name TEXT NOT NULL,
  country       TEXT NOT NULL,
  open_date     TEXT NOT NULL,
  status        TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (status IN ('ACTIVE','CLOSED','FROZEN'))
);
CREATE TABLE Transactions (
  txn_id           INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  account_id       INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES Accounts(account_id),
  txn_time         TEXT NOT NULL,        -- 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS'
  amount           REAL NOT NULL,        -- negative = refund
  channel          TEXT NOT NULL,
  merchant_country TEXT NOT NULL
);
CREATE TABLE AccountProfiles (
  account_id         INTEGER PRIMARY KEY REFERENCES Accounts(account_id),
  risk_tier          TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (risk_tier IN ('LOW','MEDIUM','HIGH')),
  avg_monthly_spend  REAL,               -- NULL when unknown
  home_country       TEXT NOT NULL
);
CREATE TABLE RiskAlerts (
  alert_id   INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  txn_id     INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES Transactions(txn_id),
  alert_type TEXT NOT NULL,
  severity   TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (severity IN ('LOW','MEDIUM','HIGH','CRITICAL')),
  created_at TEXT NOT NULL,
  resolved   INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK (resolved IN (0,1))
);
questions.starterQuery:
SELECT a.account_id, a.customer_name, COUNT(*) AS txn_count, 0.0 AS total_amount, 0.0 AS largest_txn
FROM Accounts a
JOIN Transactions t ON t.account_id = a.account_id
-- TODO: filters, GROUP BY, HAVING, ORDER BY
;
questions.outputSpec: Columns, in order: account_id, customer_name, txn_count, total_amount, largest_txn. Order: total_amount DESC, account_id ASC.

hiddenTests.description: Equal totals -> tie broken by account_id

solution.referenceSolution:
SELECT a.account_id, a.customer_name,
       COUNT(*)                    AS txn_count,
       ROUND(SUM(t.amount), 2)     AS total_amount,
       MAX(t.amount)               AS largest_txn
FROM Accounts a
JOIN Transactions t ON t.account_id = a.account_id
WHERE a.status = 'ACTIVE'
  AND t.txn_time >= '2025-01-01 00:00:00' AND t.txn_time < '2025-02-01 00:00:00'
  AND t.amount > 0
GROUP BY a.account_id, a.customer_name
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3
ORDER BY total_amount DESC, a.account_id ASC;
solution.explanation: Filter before grouping (status, half-open date range, amount > 0), group per account and apply HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3. A BETWEEN '2025-01-01' AND '2025-01-31' filter would miss late-January timestamps.

questions.title: Alert Rate by Risk Tier
questions.statement:
Using `Transactions`, `AccountProfiles` and `RiskAlerts`, summarise purchases by the account's `risk_tier`.

Consider only transactions with `amount > 0` that belong to an account **having a profile**. A transaction is *flagged* if it has **at least one** row in `RiskAlerts` (any type, resolved or not). Note that a transaction can have several alerts.

Return one row per risk tier that has such transactions:

`risk_tier, txn_count, flagged_count, flag_rate, max_amount`

* `txn_count` – number of distinct qualifying transactions
* `flagged_count` – number of distinct qualifying transactions that are flagged
* `flag_rate` – `flagged_count / txn_count` rounded to 4 decimals
* `max_amount` – largest qualifying amount in the tier

Order tiers `HIGH`, `MEDIUM`, `LOW`.

questions.starterQuery:
SELECT p.risk_tier, COUNT(*) AS txn_count, 0 AS flagged_count, 0.0 AS flag_rate, MAX(t.amount) AS max_amount
FROM Transactions t
JOIN AccountProfiles p ON p.account_id = t.account_id
-- TODO: LEFT JOIN alerts, avoid double counting
GROUP BY p.risk_tier;
questions.outputSpec: Columns, in order: risk_tier, txn_count, flagged_count, flag_rate, max_amount. Order HIGH, MEDIUM, LOW.

hiddenTests.description: Accounts without a profile and transactions without alerts only
Multiple alerts on one transaction must not inflate counts

solution.referenceSolution:
SELECT p.risk_tier,
       COUNT(DISTINCT t.txn_id) AS txn_count,
       COUNT(DISTINCT a.txn_id) AS flagged_count,
       ROUND(1.0 * COUNT(DISTINCT a.txn_id) / COUNT(DISTINCT t.txn_id), 4) AS flag_rate,
       MAX(t.amount) AS max_amount
FROM Transactions t
JOIN AccountProfiles p ON p.account_id = t.account_id
LEFT JOIN RiskAlerts a ON a.txn_id = t.txn_id
WHERE t.amount > 0
GROUP BY p.risk_tier
ORDER BY CASE p.risk_tier WHEN 'HIGH' THEN 1 WHEN 'MEDIUM' THEN 2 ELSE 3 END;
solution.explanation: LEFT JOIN alerts so un-alerted transactions stay in the denominator, and use COUNT(DISTINCT ...) because one transaction with 3 alerts produces 3 joined rows. CASE gives the required tier order.

hiddenTests.description: NULL average, missing profile, just above/below 3x, resolved and non-HIGH alerts

solution.referenceSolution:
UPDATE RiskAlerts
SET severity = 'CRITICAL'
WHERE resolved = 0
  AND severity = 'HIGH'
  AND (SELECT t.amount FROM Transactions t WHERE t.txn_id = RiskAlerts.txn_id)
      > 3 * (SELECT p.avg_monthly_spend
             FROM Transactions t JOIN AccountProfiles p ON p.account_id = t.account_id
             WHERE t.txn_id = RiskAlerts.txn_id);
solution.explanation: Correlated scalar subqueries fetch the amount and the profile's average spend for each alert. When a profile is missing or the average is NULL the comparison is NULL and the alert is not updated, which is exactly the required behaviour.

questions.title: Join Transactions to Account Risk Features
questions.statement:
Implement `join_txn_features(txns, accounts)` that enriches transactions with account attributes and simple time/geography flags.

1. Parse `txn_time` using format `%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S`; **drop** rows that cannot be parsed.
2. If a `txn_id` occurs more than once, **keep the first occurrence** (in input order).
3. **Left-join** `accounts` (unique `account_id`; columns `risk_tier`, `home_country`) onto the transactions.
4. Create `hour` (0–23, int64), `is_night` (`hour < 6` or `hour >= 22`) and `is_foreign` (`True` only when the account is known and `merchant_country != home_country`; `False` for unknown accounts).
5. Fill missing `risk_tier` with `'UNKNOWN'`.

Return columns `txn_id, account_id, amount, hour, is_night, is_foreign, risk_tier` sorted by `txn_id`, with default index.

comparison.dtypePolicy: Values compared by category: numeric (int/float interchangeable), bool, datetime, str; nulls (NaN/NaT/None/pd.NA) equal each other.

publicTests.description: Sample: unknown account, bad timestamp, duplicate id, boundary hours
Unknown account only and a US customer shopping in the US

solution.referenceSolution:
import pandas as pd

def join_txn_features(txns, accounts):
    df = txns.copy()
    df["txn_time"] = pd.to_datetime(df["txn_time"], format="%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S", errors="coerce")
    df = df.dropna(subset=["txn_time"]).drop_duplicates(subset="txn_id", keep="first")
    df = df.merge(accounts[["account_id", "risk_tier", "home_country"]], on="account_id", how="left")
    df["hour"] = df["txn_time"].dt.hour.astype("int64")
    df["is_night"] = (df["hour"] < 6) | (df["hour"] >= 22)
    df["is_foreign"] = (df["home_country"].notna() & (df["merchant_country"] != df["home_country"])).astype(bool)
    df["risk_tier"] = df["risk_tier"].fillna("UNKNOWN")
    return df.sort_values("txn_id")[["txn_id", "account_id", "amount", "hour", "is_night", "is_foreign", "risk_tier"]].reset_index(drop=True)
solution.explanation: Parse with errors='coerce' and drop NaT, deduplicate on txn_id, left-merge accounts. The boolean flags are vectorised comparisons; unknown accounts have NaN home_country so notna() makes is_foreign False.

solution.referenceSolution:
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

def velocity_features(txns):
    df = txns.copy()
    df["txn_time"] = pd.to_datetime(df["txn_time"])
    df = df.sort_values(["account_id", "txn_time", "txn_id"], kind="mergesort").reset_index(drop=True)
    df["mins_since_prev"] = df.groupby("account_id")["txn_time"].diff().dt.total_seconds() / 60.0
    counts, sums = [], []
    for _, g in df.groupby("account_id", sort=False):
        t = g.set_index("txn_time")["amount"]
        roll = t.rolling("60min")          # window (t-60min, t], rows up to the current position only
        counts.append(roll.count().to_numpy()); sums.append(roll.sum().to_numpy())
    df["txn_count_1h"] = pd.Series(np.concatenate(counts) if counts else [], dtype="float64").astype("int64") if len(df) else pd.Series([], dtype="int64")
    df["amt_sum_1h"] = np.concatenate(sums) if sums else np.array([], dtype="float64")
    return df[["txn_id", "account_id", "mins_since_prev", "txn_count_1h", "amt_sum_1h"]]
solution.explanation: Sort, use groupby().diff() for the gap and a time-based rolling('60min') per account. pandas' default window is (t-60min, t], which matches the specification and excludes rows exactly 60 minutes old; equal timestamps only see earlier rows in the sort order.

solution.referenceSolution:
import pandas as pd

def risk_summary(txns):
    df = txns.dropna(subset=["amount"]).copy()
    df["night_amount"] = df["amount"].where(df["is_night"], 0.0)
    out = (df.groupby("account_id", as_index=False)
             .agg(n_txn=("amount", "size"), total_amount=("amount", "sum"), max_amount=("amount", "max"),
                  pct_night=("is_night", "mean"), night_total=("night_amount", "sum")))
    out = out[out["n_txn"] >= 2]
    return out.sort_values(["total_amount", "account_id"], ascending=[False, True]).reset_index(drop=True)
solution.explanation: Named aggregation on the cleaned frame; a helper column masks non-night amounts so night_total is a plain sum. Filtering n_txn >= 2 happens after aggregation.

questions.title: Balanced Fraud/Normal Windows
questions.statement:
A stream of events is encoded as a string: `'F'` = flagged-fraud event, `'N'` = confirmed-normal event, and any other lowercase letter is an unrelated event. A **window** is a non-empty contiguous substring.

Return the number of windows that contain **exactly as many `'F'` as `'N'` characters** (windows containing neither count, because 0 = 0). Count windows by position: identical substrings at different positions are different windows.
constraints: s consists of lowercase letters and uppercase 'F' and 'N'

examples.description: 'FFNN' (whole minus x), 'FN' (middle) and 'x' alone are balanced, plus 'FFNNx' itself -> 4 windows

questions.expectedComplexity: O(n) time, O(n) space (prefix balance + hash map)

hiddenTests.description: No F or N at all
All F then all N, n=100000

solution.explanation: Let balance = (#F - #N) over a prefix. A window (i, j] is balanced exactly when prefix balances at i and j are equal. Scan once, keeping a hash map from balance to number of earlier prefixes with that balance; each new prefix adds that many windows.

Each transaction batch has an audit window `[start, end]` (inclusive integer times, `start < end`). An auditor can sample the system at chosen **distinct integer times**. Every window must contain **at least two** of the chosen times.

Return the minimum number of distinct times that must be chosen so that every window contains at least two of them. Windows may be given in any order and may repeat.

solution.referenceSolution:
from typing import List

def min_audit_times(windows: List[List[int]]) -> int:
    iv = sorted(windows, key=lambda w: (w[1], -w[0]))
    a = b = -10**18            # the two latest chosen times, a < b
    count = 0
    for s, e in iv:
        if s > b:              # no chosen time inside the window
            count += 2; a, b = e - 1, e
        elif s > a:            # only b is inside
            count += 1; a, b = b, e
    return count
solution.explanation: Greedy: sort windows by right end (ties: larger start first). Maintain the two most recently chosen times a < b. If the next window contains neither, choose its last two points (e-1, e); if it contains only b, choose e. Choosing as late as possible leaves maximum overlap with later windows, which is optimal by an exchange argument.
